title: Collider-quality plasma wakefield acceleration

concept.text: The innovation would be an integrated accelerator that carries an electron bunch through successive plasma acceleration stages while preserving the beam quality needed for demanding applications. A laser pulse or energetic particle bunch drives a strong electric wake in plasma; a trailing electron bunch gains energy from that wake. The goal is to repeat that energy gain through independent stages without losing useful charge, increasing the beam's energy spread excessively, or degrading its emittance, which measures how tightly the particles remain organized in position and direction.

The defining capability is the simultaneous delivery of high energy, narrow energy spread, low emittance, useful charge, adequate efficiency, repetition rate and stable operation. The supplied FACET-II experiment demonstrates substantial progress within an injector-accelerator system. Its three plasma sections perform focusing, injection and acceleration; they do not establish transport of the same bunch through successive independent energy-gain stages. Collider-quality plasma acceleration remains the broader integration goal described here, rather than an achieved system in the supplied evidence.

significance.text: Plasma acceleration offers a physical route to much shorter high-energy accelerating sections. The supplied experiment reports an effective average accelerating gradient of 13 GeV per meter, while its discussion places radio-frequency cavity breakdown limits near 100 MV per meter. These figures illustrate the gradient advantage, although a cavity limit and an experimental plasma gradient are not directly comparable measures of an entire accelerator facility. Sustaining high plasma gradients while preserving beam quality through repeated stages could substantially change the scale of high-energy electron accelerators.

The direct benefit would be a more compact means of supplying high-quality energetic electron beams. The paper identifies future coherent light sources and collider concepts as prospective applications. Complete light sources would still need the systems that turn the electron beam into useful radiation; a high-luminosity collider would additionally need collision systems and a suitable operating architecture. Demonstrating tens-of-GeV electron acceleration would therefore be an enabling milestone, with TeV operation and a particle-physics program conditional on further scaling and integration.

Impact assessment: a large reduction in accelerating length does not establish an equally large reduction in total facility size or cost. Drivers, interstage beam transport, power conversion, diagnostics and supporting infrastructure must be included in that comparison. The earlier estimate of a one- or two-order-of-magnitude reduction in total size and cost is not established by the supplied evidence. Broader access to high-energy beams is a plausible downstream possibility if the complete system proves economical and reliable.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this record is reproducible, staged acceleration with the required beam properties delivered together. High energy gain alone is insufficient: an accelerator must preserve narrow energy spread and low emittance while carrying enough charge to be useful. The supplied paper explicitly connects future collider operation to hundreds of picocoulombs per bunch, efficient energy transfer from the driver to the trailing bunch, and luminosity at a practical repetition rate. Those requirements interact, so optimizing a selected high-energy, low-charge pulse does not by itself resolve the system problem.

Engineering synthesis: successive stages must accept, focus and synchronize the same bunch, restore the accelerating conditions and deliver further energy gain without accumulating unacceptable beam degradation. Interstage transport must be included in the compactness budget. Injection variability, alignment and timing tolerances, plasma reproducibility, and control of the energy distribution must be managed across many pulses and stages. These are concrete integration barriers; the supplied evidence does not establish their solution in a complete staged linac.

Reliable output and efficiency remain distinct from the existence of a high-gradient wake. The FACET-II study operated its linac and pulsed gas jet at 5 Hz, but its reported injection and high-energy-gain fractions show that operation at a stated repetition rate is not equivalent to delivering the desired beam on every pulse. Likewise, large energy losses by some drive electrons and an energy transformer ratio above two do not alone establish efficient delivery of useful trailing-bunch energy or favorable overall power consumption.

Scope synthesis: an electron-only staged demonstration would leave the requirements of an electron–positron collider unresolved, including positron acceleration and preservation of positron beam quality. Collision luminosity, long-duration availability and full-system power requirements would also need separate demonstrations. The appropriate numerical requirements depend on the intended collider or light-source design; the supplied material does not establish a universal operating-duration or stability threshold.

current_state.text: On 28 November 2025, Zhang, Storey, Knetsch and colleagues reported FACET-II experiments using a conventional 10 GeV drive bunch and a meter-scale plasma source with focusing, injection and acceleration sections. The study reported injected electron bunches above 20 GeV with sub-percent energy spread and an effective average accelerating gradient of 13 GeV per meter. This is a published component-level achievement within one experimental campaign, rather than a demonstration of successive independent accelerator stages.

The reported normalized emittance measurements ranged from 1.9 to 5 mm·mrad, with a reported mean of 3.2 ± 2.0 mm·mrad. Thus, about 2 mm·mrad describes the low end of the measured results rather than uniform output. Peak currents of 0.3–3.9 kA were reconstructed using an inverse-model approach because the available apparatus could not directly measure all relevant bunch properties. The multi-kA current result should consequently be understood as model-inferred. The strongest energy, spread, emittance and current figures should not be read as a guarantee that every pulse simultaneously achieved them.

The study also reported an energy transformer ratio exceeding two and a brightness enhancement exceeding an order of magnitude. Some drive electrons lost about 90% or more of their initial energy. The drive-depletion measurements used separate shots, so they do not establish that maximal depletion and the strongest trailing-bunch properties occurred together on a single pulse. The transformer ratio concerns the relative energy gain and loss; it is not itself a measurement of the fraction of total driver energy converted into useful accelerated-bunch energy.

The FACET-II linac and pulsed gas jet operated at 5 Hz. Injection detection probability was approximately 15%, and approximately 15% of shots in the best datasets showed energy gains above 15 GeV. These are separately reported performance statistics and should not be combined into an inferred overall success rate. The study did not demonstrate sustained delivery at 5 Hz of beams meeting all its headline quality values, nor did it demonstrate collider luminosity or positron acceleration. Its dependence on a conventional drive linac applies to this beam-driven experiment; it should not be generalized to laser-driven plasma acceleration.

The supplied review assessed the complete extracted main article text and textual figure captions. Earlier research encountered a Nature identity-provider redirect, but the later source record retained verified, untruncated main-article HTML and PDF extracts. Figures and linked supplements were not assessed as inspected visual evidence. One supplementary PDF had extraction warnings, and retained supplementary material should not be treated as fully reviewed merely because it was saved.

The supplied material does not establish field-wide progress through 1 November 2026: its bounded freshness-search record is empty. It also provides no retained artifact for the cited 2024 Physical Review Accelerators and Beams paper, so that paper's proposed quotation and detailed support could not be checked in the supplied review. EuPRAXIA's claimed 2026 technical-design status has no supporting text here and remains unverified. These limitations restrict the breadth and currency of this account; they do not invalidate the dated FACET-II result.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed intermediate demonstration: transport the same electron bunch through successive independent plasma energy-gain stages and measure an exit energy of at least tens of GeV, sub-percent energy spread and normalized emittance of a few mm·mrad or better. Demonstrate operation above 1 Hz over a specified, published operating period. These numerical thresholds are proposed milestones, not established collider specifications. Merely dividing a single injector-accelerator into focusing, injection and acceleration sections would not satisfy the independent-staging requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Independent stages deliver tens-of-GeV bunches meeting quality and repetition-rate thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reliability and reproducibility evidence: publish delivered charge, distributions of exit beam parameters, the fraction of pulses meeting all stated thresholds simultaneously, uptime and interruptions throughout the operating period. Distinguish direct measurements from model reconstructions and report their uncertainties. Repeat the result over separate operating runs and provide enough methods and diagnostic information for independent checking and reproduction. A selected record shot or simulated exit beam would not satisfy this demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Separate runs reproduce measured beam performance with published reliability evidence

completion_criteria.text: Proposed compactness and efficiency comparison: demonstrate an accelerating length, including interstage transport, at least ten times shorter than a specified radio-frequency linac delivering the same energy. State the comparison's beam-charge, beam-quality and operating assumptions. Report energy transfer into the useful accelerated bunch and the broader driver and facility energy requirements, with their accounting boundaries. Claims about total facility size or cost would require a separate comparison that includes drivers and supporting infrastructure.
completion_criteria.label: Tenfold shorter accelerating length than comparable RF linacs, with energy accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed boundary for broader completion: the intermediate milestone would establish demonstrated staged electron-beam performance over the tested conditions. Collider readiness would require application-specific charge, efficiency, stability, repetition-rate and luminosity targets, along with positron performance where the collider architecture requires it. The supplied evidence does not determine those numerical targets. Finite demonstrations would establish a measured operating range, rather than performance at arbitrary energies, charges, durations or numbers of stages.
completion_criteria.label: Reported operating limits distinguish staged electron performance from collider readiness

related_concepts.text: Roster synthesis — PHY-12, Experimental identification of the physics that sets the Higgs-mass scale, has the clearest potential connection to the collider application: a future accelerator could support experiments probing that physics. PHY-04, Laboratory identification of the dark-matter particle, and PHY-06, Discovery of a magnetic monopole, could also benefit from suitable high-energy experiments if the relevant particles and interactions fall within reach. PHY-10 supplies an accelerator capability; none of those discoveries follows from achieving it, and their experimental routes need not depend on plasma acceleration.

Roster synthesis — PHY-07, Observation of baryon-number violation; PHY-08, Observation of lepton-number violation; and PHY-13, A tested mechanism for the cosmic matter excess, concern distinct physical observations or explanations. Better accelerators might contribute to some relevant searches, but staged plasma acceleration establishes neither symmetry violation nor a mechanism producing the cosmic matter excess. These entries retain separate scientific completion conditions.

Roster synthesis — PHY-09, A coherent gamma-ray source, overlaps through the possible use of bright energetic electron beams in photon-generation systems. Preserving electron-beam quality could support future radiation sources, but an electron accelerator alone does not demonstrate coherent gamma-ray emission. The supplied paper's discussion of coherent light sources does not establish completion of PHY-09.

Roster synthesis — PHY-02, Sustained net-electric power from controlled fusion, also involves plasma physics, but its goal is sustained net electricity rather than controlled energy transfer into a particle beam. PHY-01, Ambient-pressure superconducting conductors at room temperature, could affect accelerator components or infrastructure, but it is a separate materials breakthrough and is not demonstrated or required by the supplied plasma-acceleration result.

Roster synthesis — PHY-03, A laboratory proof that gravity is non-classical; PHY-05, A tested microphysical account of the dark-energy scale; and PHY-11, A tested resolution of the black-hole information paradox, address different foundational questions. More capable experimental tools might eventually contribute, but the supplied material establishes no direct enabling relationship between those outcomes and PHY-10. They remain independent entries.

change_log.reason: The paper's three-function source does not demonstrate the central multistage integration goal.

change_log.reason: Operating repetition rate and sustained delivery of beams meeting all quality thresholds are different achievements.

change_log.change: Expanded the emittance result to its reported range and mean, identified reconstructed current, and qualified drive depletion as measured on separate shots.
change_log.reason: Selected low emittance, model-inferred peak current and depletion results should not imply uniform or simultaneous pulse performance.

change_log.change: Separated the energy transformer ratio and drive depletion from useful energy-transfer efficiency.
change_log.reason: Neither quantity alone establishes efficient conversion of total driver energy into the accelerated bunch.

change_log.change: Retained the high-gradient compactness argument while removing an asserted one- or two-order-of-magnitude total size-and-cost reduction.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports much shorter accelerating sections conditionally, without establishing corresponding whole-facility savings.

change_log.change: Restricted conventional drive-linac dependence to the documented FACET-II experiment and qualified EuPRAXIA and November 2026 field-wide status.
change_log.reason: The original wording generalized beyond the experiment, and the supplied record does not support the EuPRAXIA or freshness claims.

change_log.change: Recast the proposed completion test as an intermediate milestone and added successful-pulse fractions, charge, efficiency, repeated runs and explicit comparison boundaries.
change_log.reason: Tens-of-GeV electron operation above 1 Hz would not alone establish collider readiness, and the proposal needs assessable reliability and compactness conditions.

unresolved_issues: Field-wide progress after the November 2025 FACET-II publication remains unassessed through 1 November 2026 because the supplied freshness-search record is empty.
EuPRAXIA's 2026 technical-design status and the detailed support of the cited 2024 APS paper remain unverified in the supplied material.
The supplied review does not establish the fraction of pulses simultaneously meeting the headline energy, energy-spread, emittance, charge and current values.

Application-specific thresholds for charge, efficiency, successful-pulse fraction, operating duration and acceptable stability remain to be selected; the proposed intermediate criteria do not resolve them.
Independent staging, scaling toward TeV energies, positron performance where required, and collider luminosity remain outside the demonstrated result described here.
Whole-facility size, power and cost advantages require an integrated design and explicit comparison rather than inference from plasma gradient alone.
Figures and supplements were not inspected as visual evidence in the supplied review, and one supplementary extraction had warnings; no additional resolution of those limitations is claimed.

brief.title: Compact accelerators with precise electron beams
possible: Researchers could use much shorter accelerating sections to produce energetic electron beams for future light sources and particle colliders. The beams would keep their particles tightly organized and closely matched in energy as they passed through successive acceleration stages.

Each stage would use plasma, a gas containing freed electrons. A laser pulse or particle bunch would create an electric wake, and a following electron bunch would gain energy from it. Repeating this reliably would let the beam reach higher energies while retaining its quality.
why: Accelerator length helps make high-energy research facilities large and expensive. Plasma can accelerate electrons over much shorter distances. Preserving beam quality through repeated stages could change the scale of the accelerating sections needed for these facilities.
Compact sources of high-quality electron beams could support future light sources for scientific research and collider designs for studying particles and forces.

sources.who: Chaojie Zhang, Douglas Storey, Alexander Knetsch and colleagues
sources.showed: At FACET-II, the team produced electron bunches above 20 billion electronvolts with closely matched energies. Their plasma system combined beam focusing, electron injection and acceleration.
sources.quote: Here we demonstrate that a plasma wakefield accelerator can be used as a transformer to simultaneously boost the energy and brightness of a self-injected electron bunch.
sources.cited_for: Plasma acceleration can deliver high electron energies while improving how tightly the beam's particles are organized.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not carry the same bunch through independent energy-gain stages or demonstrate reliable delivery of all required beam properties together.

shown: Zhang and colleagues at FACET-II produced electron bunches above 20 billion electronvolts with a narrow range of particle energies. This was an achievement within one experimental campaign. The system's focusing, injection and acceleration sections were not independent energy-gain stages.

Beam tightness varied between measurements, and peak current was inferred using a model. The strongest reported properties were not demonstrated together as sustained output. Large energy losses by driving electrons also did not establish efficient transfer into the useful beam.
missing: The same bunch must gain energy through independent stages while retaining enough charge, closely matched energies and tightly organized particles.
Separate runs must reliably deliver all required beam properties together, with measured success rates and interruptions.
A complete system must demonstrate useful energy transfer and compactness while including transport between stages and driver power.
Collider operation still requires suitable collision rates and stability, plus acceleration of positrons, the electron's antiparticles, where needed.

milestones.label: Independent stages deliver energetic beams with preserved quality
milestones.explanation: The same bunch would have to cross independent stages, meet the proposed energy and beam-quality targets, and operate above one pulse per second over a stated period. This would establish staged performance.

milestones.label: Separate runs reproduce beam performance with measured reliability
milestones.explanation: Separate runs would have to report delivered charge, beam-property distributions, simultaneous success rates, uptime and measurement uncertainties. Reproducible methods would let others assess whether the performance holds.

milestones.label: Tenfold shorter acceleration with explicit energy accounting
milestones.explanation: The accelerating length, including transport between stages, would have to be tenfold shorter than a comparable conventional accelerator. Useful-beam energy transfer and driver and facility energy needs would also be reported.

milestones.label: Measured operating limits define the remaining collider requirements
milestones.explanation: Results would have to define the tested operating range and distinguish it from application-specific collider requirements, including positrons where needed. This would establish what staged electron performance actually supports.

uncertain: The fraction of pulses simultaneously meeting all headline beam properties remains unknown.
Required charge, efficiency, stability, successful-pulse fraction and operating duration depend on the intended application.
Whole-facility size, power and cost advantages remain uncertain until drivers and supporting infrastructure are included.

page.title: Multi-GeV staging of plasma wakefield accelerators
page.definition: An electron bunch gains multi-GeV energy in successive plasma stages, each powered by an independent driver. The ionized gas supports an electric wake; more than 90% of the bunch is captured, its emittance (transverse position–momentum area) is preserved, and energy gain per total stage-and-transport length exceeds 5 GeV/m.

goal.need: Linear colliders typically require electron energies of 100 GeV or more. Laser- and electron-driven plasma stages have finite driver energy, so the field pursues staging to combine multiple drivers. Interstage transport must retain the accelerated charge and emittance without consuming the gradient advantage shown below.

figures.caption: Field and gradient figures motivating plasma acceleration
figures.note: The RF figure is a cavity field limit; the plasma figure is an effective experimental gradient. Neither is a whole-facility gradient.

statements.body: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
statements.quote: Sequentially combining plasma wakefield accelerators to reach successively higher energies is an attractive path to future high energy physics particle colliders.

statements.body: SPARTA, the European Research Council-funded University of Oslo programme
statements.quote: The goal of the ERC-funded project SPARTA is to solve the staging and stability problems of plasma acceleration
statements.context: Programme objectives stated in a preprint submitted on 20 May 2025.

completion.title: Independent plasma stages give >5 GeV/m with >90% capture and preserve electron emittance.
completion.criterion: The same electron bunch undergoes multi-GeV acceleration through independently driven plasma stages using equal-energy drive beams, with capture efficiency >90%, average/geometric accelerating gradient >5 GV/m and preserved emittance between stages. The roadmap gives 5 GeV + 5 GeV as an example, not a mandatory energy pair. Geometric gradient includes interstage transport.
completion.set_by: DOE Office of High Energy Physics, Advanced Accelerator Concepts Research Roadmap Workshop report, page 3. This numerical specification was written for laser-driven stages.
completion.threshold_quote: high beam capture efficiency (>90%), while maintaining a large average/geometric accelerating gradient (>5 GV/m) and preserving the beam emittance between LWFA stages.
completion.basis: This published experiment tests the staging capability defined here by combining charge capture, emittance preservation and geometric gradient. It is a collider-development target. Collider operation additionally requires architecture-specific charge, energy spread, efficiency, repetition rate and collision luminosity.

milestones.title: Electrons gain measurable energy from a driver-excited plasma wake.
milestones.criterion: Measure electron energy gain caused by a driver-excited plasma wake. Electron-driven evidence, published 4 July 1988: a 21 MeV driver excited megavolt-per-metre wakes probed by a delayed 15 MeV witness. Laser-driven evidence, published 3 August 1998: externally injected electrons gained up to 1.6 MeV. These laboratory demonstrations did not require preservation of beam quality.
milestones.set_by: Experimental plasma-acceleration convention: observing witness-electron acceleration, exemplified by the Argonne and LULI experiments.
milestones.threshold_quote: The acceleration of electrons injected in a plasma wave generated by the laser wakefield mechanism has been observed.

milestones.title: A plasma stage preserves measured emittance, charge and energy spread while accelerating electrons.
milestones.criterion: Acceleration preserves measured normalized emittance within fit error while preserving charge and relative energy spread. Electron-driven evidence, published 19 July 2024: FLASHForward measured horizontal emittance 2.85 ± 0.07 before and 2.80 ± 0.09 mm·mrad after acceleration, using 210 reference and 420 plasma shots; energy gain reached 40 MeV at about 40 pC. Charge and spread lay within their initial 68th-percentile ranges in 41% and 62% of shots, respectively. Vertical emittance was not measured.
milestones.set_by: Plasma-accelerator preservation convention, applied experimentally by the FLASHForward collaboration in Figure 2; the demonstrated emittance test concerned the horizontal plane.
milestones.threshold_quote: was preserved to within the fit error.

milestones.title: A plasma stage adds >10 GeV with <2% energy spread and preserved emittance.
milestones.criterion: One plasma stage adds >10 GeV with >80% driver-to-wake efficiency, >40% wake-to-bunch efficiency, <2% final energy spread and preserved emittance, simultaneously. Electron-driven evidence, published 28 November 2025: one injected bunch reached 26 GeV, 0.7% rms spread and 2.3 pC; the joint test was not demonstrated. Laser-driven evidence, published 18 December 2024: a selected spectrum peaked at 9.2 GeV with charge beyond 10 GeV; the joint test was not demonstrated.
milestones.set_by: FACET-II plasma-wakefield experimental programme, Storey et al., Introduction. The joint target was written for electron-bunch-driven acceleration.
milestones.threshold_quote: achieving a final energy spread of <2% and the emittance preservation after acceleration.

milestones.title: Independent plasma stages give multi-GeV electron acceleration with 90% beam capture.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate multi-GeV electron acceleration through separate plasma stages, with independent equal-energy drive beams and 90% beam capture. Laser-driven evidence, published 1 February 2016: a subset gained about 100 MeV in a second independently driven stage, with 1.2 pC accelerated charge and 3.5% trapping efficiency; delay-scan spectra averaged five shots per point. Electron-driven evidence, published 28 November 2025: FACET-II's focusing, injection and acceleration sections form one injector–accelerator, not independently driven stages.
milestones.set_by: DOE Office of High Energy Physics, Advanced Accelerator Concepts Research Roadmap Workshop report, common challenge 1, pages 2–3; applicable to laser- and particle-beam-driven plasma acceleration.

not_found: No experimental report satisfying the complete multi-GeV staging test was found.
No architecture-independent numerical certification of collider readiness was found in the DOE roadmap, National Academies report or staging reviews.
The DOE staging target does not specify an emittance-growth tolerance, successful-pulse fraction or operating duration.
No laser-driven experiment meeting the joint emittance, charge and energy-spread preservation test was identified.
The complete European Accelerator R&D Roadmap could not be opened from CERN or arXiv.
The full 1988 and 1998 laboratory-demonstration papers could not be opened; their accessible abstracts omit shot counts.

results.finding: LWFA electron bunches reached a mean peak energy of 716 MeV; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The laser-driven first stage generated and accelerated the electron bunches through self-truncated ionization injection.

results.finding: Electron-driven wake accelerated witness electrons by up to about 1.3 GeV; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The witness electrons were injected internally into the wake driven by the LWFA-generated bunch.
results.quote:
The highest measured electron energy gain is around

results.finding: A hybrid two-stage accelerator produced witnesses reaching 1.3 GeV; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The first-stage bunch drives the second stage, where a new witness is injected. The same bunch was not accelerated through both stages, and neither independent equal-energy drivers nor 90% capture was demonstrated.
results.quote: Here, we address several of these challenges simultaneously using a hybrid scheme in which an electron bunch from a laser wakefield accelerator (LWFA) drives a subsequent plasma wakefield accelerator (PWFA) stage with internal witness injection.

results.finding: Laser-driven plasma stage: well-aligned shots, number unspecified, reached a maximum electron energy of 10.2 GeV.
results.detail: The experiment does not establish the required driver-to-wake and wake-to-bunch efficiencies, final energy spread, and preserved emittance simultaneously. The 10.2 GeV figure is a maximum electron energy.
results.quote: Shots that were well aligned to the electron spectrometer indicated a maximum energy of 10.2 GeV.

results.finding: Laser-driven plasma acceleration, 50 shots: electron spectrum tails extended beyond 10 GeV.
results.detail: The >10 GeV result concerns spectral tails, not the whole bunch. The paper does not demonstrate the required driver-to-wake and wake-to-bunch efficiencies, final energy spread, and preserved emittance simultaneously.
results.quote: The high energy tails range to above 10 GeV, with charge ~10 pC above 9 GeV.

results.finding: Electron bunches: in 800 events, 30% showed an energy gain above 30 GeV.
results.detail: The gain was achieved by electrons in the tail of the same pulse that drove the wake. The text does not establish the required efficiencies, final energy spread, and emittance preservation simultaneously.
results.quote:
With this plasma length, in a series of 800 events, 30%
showed an energy gain of more than 30 GeV.
